title: Appointing a director at a general meeting
law: Sections 152, 153, 160, 164, 165, 170 and 189; Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014
summary: A person is appointed as director by ordinary resolution of the members, after notice of candidature, checks on DIN and disqualification, and a filing with the Registrar.
when: When the company wants members to appoint a new director at an annual general meeting.
applies: Public companies in full; private companies skip the notice, deposit, stock exchange and refund steps

steps.d: The candidate, or a member proposing the candidate, gives written notice at the company's office. The notice must reach the company at least 14 days before the meeting and carry a deposit of Rs. 1,00,000.
steps.time: At least 14 days before the meeting

steps.d: On receiving the notice, serve an individual notice on every member about the candidature, at least 7 days before the meeting.
steps.time: At least 7 days before the meeting

steps.d: If individual notice is not practicable, publish the notice in two newspapers, one English and one regional language, circulating where the registered office is. Publish at least 7 days before the meeting.
steps.time: At least 7 days before the meeting

steps.d: A listed company sends a copy of the notice to the stock exchange where it is listed.
Confirm the person is not disqualified under Section 164 and does not breach the directorship limits in Section 165.
If the person has no DIN, they must apply in Form DIR-3. Make sure the person tells the company the DIN.
Collect the person's consent and declaration in Form DIR-2 before the meeting.

At the AGM pass an ordinary resolution to appoint the director and authorise someone to sign Form DIR-12. If there are several proposals for non-retiring persons, take up and decide each one separately.
A listed company sends the proceedings of the AGM to the stock exchange, as Schedule III of the SEBI Listing Regulations requires.
If the person is appointed, refund the Rs. 1,00,000 deposit to the person or to the member who proposed them.

Sign the form digitally by the managing director, manager or company secretary of the company. A practising CA, CS or cost accountant must also certify it digitally. Attach the appointment letter, the director's Form DIR-2 and the interest in other entities. Add the first-director declaration where it applies.
A listed company gives the stock exchange the particulars of the appointment.
Enter the director's particulars in the registers under Sections 170 and 189.
The new director tells every other company where they are a director about the appointment.

forms.purpose: Application for a DIN, if the person has none
Consent and declaration of the proposed director
Particulars of appointment of director to the Registrar

checklist: Written notice of candidature with Rs. 1,00,000 deposit (public company)
Individual notice or newspaper notice to members

meetings.title: Annual general meeting to appoint the director
meetings.notice_days: 21 clear days (shorter with consent of members as the Act allows)

resolutions.title: Appointment of a director
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT pursuant to Sections 152 and 160 and other applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, [name of person] (DIN [number]), who has given consent and a declaration of no disqualification, be and is hereby appointed as a Director of {co}, liable to retire by rotation. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name], Director / Company Secretary, be authorised to sign and file Form DIR-12 and do all things needed to give effect to this resolution.
resolutions.explanatory: Under Section 102, state: the notice of candidature received from [name of member / candidate] on [date] under Section 160; the deposit received; the candidate's profile, qualifications and other directorships; and that the director's consent in Form DIR-2 is on file.

docs.title: Notice of candidature for director
paras: To the Board of Directors, {co}, [registered office address].

I, [name of member / candidate], give notice under Section 160 of the Companies Act, 2013 that I intend to propose / offer myself as a candidate for the office of Director of {co} at the general meeting to be held on [date].
A deposit of Rs. 1,00,000 is enclosed by [cheque / transfer details]. Signed: [name], [date].

flags: The reference note does not cite Section 160 for the notice and deposit rules, although these come from it. The deposit is also refunded if the candidate gets 25% or more of the valid votes cast, even if not elected. Verify against Section 160(1).
The reference note gives no deadline for DIR-12. The rule is 30 days from the date of appointment.
Section 160(2) and Rule 13 also require the company to put the notice on its website, if it has one. The reference note mentions only individual and newspaper notice.
The reference note lists only DIR-2 as the declaration. A separate declaration that the person is not disqualified (Form DIR-8) is also normally collected.
Step on the first-director declaration applies only to first directors of a new company, not to ordinary appointments.
Section 189 is the register of contracts, not directors; the register of directors is under Section 170. Check which register is meant.
private: Steps 1, 2, 4, 10, 11 and 13 do not apply to private companies, in the reference note's numbering.

title: Buying back shares
law: Sections 68, 69 and 70; Rule 17 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014; Articles of Association
summary: The company buys its own fully paid shares from shareholders, after approvals, solvency declaration and filings, and then cancels them.
when: When a company wants to return cash to shareholders by repurchasing its own shares.
applies: Private and public companies; the reference note gives no private-company exemptions

steps.d: See whether the Articles allow a buy-back. If not, alter them first by special resolution.
Send notice and agenda for a board meeting to consider the buy-back.
Pass the board resolution to authorise the buy-back. A buy-back of 10% or less of paid-up equity capital and free reserves can be approved by the board alone.
If the buy-back is larger than 10%, send notice for an EGM and pass a special resolution there.
The total value of shares bought back must not exceed 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves.
After the buy-back, total secured and unsecured debt must not exceed twice the paid-up capital and free reserves.
Only fully paid-up shares and other specified securities can be bought back.
File the board or special resolution with the Registrar.
steps.time: Within 30 days of passing the resolution

steps.d: Get the auditor's buy-back certificate and the latest financials, and file Form SH-8 with the Registrar.
Collect the directors' affidavit of declaration of solvency and file Form SH-9 with the Registrar.

steps.t: Pay the seller through the AD bank
steps.d: Where the seller is a non-resident, file papers with the authorised dealer bank: Form A2, debit authority letter, Forms 15CA and 15CB, valuation certificate, offer and acceptance letters, declarations, KYC, share certificate copies, shareholding before and after, bank charges letter. Resolve the bank's queries so the money can be remitted.

After payment, file Form SH-11 with the Registrar. State the dates of board resolution, opening and closing of offer, completion of buy-back and payment. When approved, the MCA master data shows the reduced paid-up capital.
Destroy the certificates of the bought-back shares.
steps.time: Within 7 days of the last date of completion

forms.purpose: Filing of board or special resolution
Letter of offer / buy-back certificate filing

checklist: Board and, if needed, EGM approvals
Latest audited and 'as on date' financials
25% limit and 2:1 debt-equity ratio worked out

meetings.title: Board meeting to approve the buy-back
meetings.notice_days: As per Section 173 and SS-1 (7 days)

meetings.title: Extraordinary general meeting for the buy-back

resolutions.title: Approval of buy-back of shares
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT pursuant to Sections 68, 69 and 70 of the Companies Act, 2013, Rule 17 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 and the Articles of Association, and subject to approval of the members where required, {co} buy back up to [number] fully paid equity shares of Rs. [face value] each at a price of Rs. [price] per share, for a total of Rs. [amount in Rs.], being [per cent]% of the paid-up capital and free reserves as per the latest audited accounts dated [date]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the offer be opened on [date] and closed on [date].

resolutions.title: Declaration of solvency and filings
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT the Directors approve the declaration of solvency in Form SH-9 and the letter of offer in Form SH-8, and that [name], Director, and [name], Director, be authorised to sign them. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name], Company Secretary, be authorised to file Forms MGT-14, SH-8, SH-9 and SH-11 and to deal with the AD bank for the remittance.

resolutions.title: Alteration of Articles to allow buy-back
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT pursuant to Section 14 and Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Articles of Association of {co} be altered by inserting a new Article [number] reading: 'The Company may purchase its own shares or other specified securities, on the terms permitted by the Act.' RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Board be authorised to file Form MGT-14 and do all acts needed.
resolutions.explanatory: Under Section 102, explain that the Articles do not now authorise a buy-back and that the alteration is needed to comply with Section 68(2)(a). Delete this resolution if the Articles already permit buy-back.

resolutions.title: Approval of buy-back above 10%
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT pursuant to Section 68(2)(b) and other applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, and the Articles of Association, the consent of the members be given to {co} to buy back up to [number] fully paid equity shares at Rs. [price] per share, for a total of Rs. [amount in Rs.], not exceeding 25% of the paid-up capital and free reserves. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Board be authorised to carry out the buy-back and file all forms.
resolutions.explanatory: Under Section 102, disclose the purpose of the buy-back, number and price, the maximum amount and its percentage of paid-up capital and free reserves, the post-buy-back debt-equity ratio, and that the buy-back will be completed within one year of this resolution.

flags: Board resolution at the EGM (step 5 of the reference note) should read special resolution; a general meeting passes a special resolution, not a board resolution.
The 10% threshold is of the aggregate of paid-up equity capital and free reserves (Section 68(2)(b)), not of equity capital alone.
The 25% cap in Section 68(2)(c) is on aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves, and for equity shares also 25% of total paid-up equity capital. Verify.

SH-8 is the letter of offer; the auditor's certificate and financials are attachments. SH-9 must be filed before the offer opens. The reference note describes SH-8 as a 'buy-back certification' filing, which looks loose.
SH-11 is due within 30 days of completing the buy-back; the reference note gives no time. Also the company must keep a register of buy-backs (Form SH-10), not named in the reference note.
The reference note says a 7-day window for destroying certificates 'from the last date of completion'; confirm against Section 68(7).
Section 69 (transfer to capital redemption reserve) and Section 70 (prohibitions, including no new issue for 6 months and a one-year gap between buy-backs) are cited but not covered; check them.
The reference note's part C on steps not applicable to private companies is empty.

title: Filing DIR-3 KYC for a director
law: Rule 12A of the Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014
summary: A director who holds a DIN updates personal details on the MCA portal in Form DIR-3 KYC, or confirms mobile number and email in the web version.
when: When a DIN holder must file or update KYC.
applies: All directors with a DIN, in private and public companies

steps.d: Click Sign In on the MCA home page. New users register first with the Register button and then log in with their user ID and password.
Go to MCA Services, Company eFiling, DIN Related Filings, then Form DIR-3 KYC. Enter the DIN, mobile number and email. Enter the OTPs sent to both and click Next.

Enter name, father's name, nationality, date of birth, gender, PAN, mobile and email with OTPs, Aadhaar number, and permanent and present residential addresses. Click Verify Income Tax PAN. A foreign national without PAN must use the same name as on the DSC.
Upload the documents, make the declaration and attach the director's DSC. A practising CA, CS or cost accountant must also sign digitally after their details are entered. Click Submit.
For DIR-3 KYC Web, log in the same way as above.
Open MCA Services, Company eFiling, DIN Related Filings, Form DIR-3 KYC Web. The email appears pre-filled. Re-enter the mobile number with country code and submit.

forms.purpose: Web-based KYC confirmation of mobile and email

checklist: Working mobile number and email for OTPs
flags: The reference note gives no filing deadline. As I understand the amended Rule 12A, the KYC web confirmation is due every year by 30 September, with the full DIR-3 KYC needed only when details change; verify the current rule and any fee for late filing.
Check the MCA portal's current menu names and whether the professional certification is still required for DIR-3 KYC.

title: Incorporating a subsidiary company
law: Section 3 (plus Sections 4, 7 and 186 as relevant); Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014
summary: The promoter, often a foreign parent, gets DSCs, reserves a name, prepares documents and files SPICe+ to incorporate an Indian subsidiary.
when: When a company, particularly a foreign one, wants to set up a subsidiary in India.
applies: Private and public companies; no private-company exemptions

steps.d: Proposed directors and subscribers obtain a DSC with 1, 2 or 3 year validity. Needed: PAN if any, passport, one of voter ID or driving licence, photo, email and phone. Foreign nationals do not need notary or legalisation for DSC papers.
Register each DSC on the MCA portal.

File Form RUN with two preferred names in order, a short note on their meaning and trademark details if any. For a foreign parent, give its name, date of incorporation, address, contact details and authorised person. Include NIC code. The name stays valid for 20 days, extendable to 60 days, or file a fresh RUN with fees.
docs: Board resolution of parent for investment in India
Board resolution and NOC for use of name

steps.d: Finalise the draft memorandum and articles with the promoters.

For each director and subscriber collect name, father's name, nationality, PAN if any, passport, residence status, occupation, education, date and place of birth, gender, mobile, email, addresses and period of stay. Also ID proof and address proof (utility bill not older than 2 months, translated if not in English). Foreign subscribers also supply signed MOA and AOA pages, INC-9 and a PAN undertaking, all notarised and legalised.

Collect the office address, whether owned or leased, title deed, owner's NOC, a recent utility bill, contact details and bank preference. If the office is not yet fixed, give a correspondence address and file Form INC-22 later.
Once the name and DSCs are ready, file SPICe+ for incorporation. PAN and TAN are applied for with it. GST and EPF registration can be taken through AGILE.
After MCA queries are answered, the Central Registration Centre issues the certificate of incorporation.

Documents must be notarised: in a Commonwealth country by a local notary; in a Hague Convention country notarised and apostilled; elsewhere notarised and authenticated by an Indian diplomatic or consular officer. No attestation is needed for a person who visited India on a business visa (not needed for persons of Indian origin or OCI holders).
If the holding company is Indian, it must follow Section 186 for the investment.
docs: Board or shareholder approval for the investment

forms.purpose: Incorporation application with PAN and TAN
Declaration by subscribers and first directors

forms.deadline: Within 30 days of incorporation, if office not given earlier

checklist: ID and address proof for each person
Parent's board resolution and NOC for name
Registered office proof and owner's NOC

meetings.title: Board meeting of the foreign parent company
meetings.notice_days: As per its own governing rules

resolutions.title: Foreign parent: investment in an Indian subsidiary
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT [name of foreign parent], a body corporate incorporated in [country], approves the incorporation of a subsidiary company in India under the name '{co}' or such other name as the Registrar may approve, with an initial subscription of [number] equity shares of face value [amount] each for Rs. [amount in Rs.]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name], [designation], be authorised to sign the MOA, AOA and all documents, to appoint directors and to act as authorised representative. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the company gives its no-objection to the use of the words '[words]' in the Indian subsidiary's name.

flags: Name reservation now generally goes through SPICe+ Part A; Form RUN is used for reserving a name separately. Verify the current MCA route.
AGILE has been replaced by AGILE-PRO-S in the later procedure; verify which form is live.
The reference note cites the Act as '2103'; it means 2013.
Foreign investment compliance (sector caps, FC-GPR reporting within 30 days of allotment) is not covered here; check FEMA rules.
The reference note lists only Section 3; incorporation also relies on Sections 4 and 7.
private: None. Setting up a subsidiary follows a standard process for every company.

title: Incorporating a company with foreign directors and subscribers
summary: A company is incorporated through SPICe+ Part A (name) and Part B (incorporation), with notarised and apostilled documents from the foreign shareholders and directors.
when: When foreign individuals or companies will be first directors or subscribers.
applies: Private and public companies, with at least one Indian resident director

steps.d: Apply with two name choices, with the right suffix (Private Limited or Public Limited), a trademark certificate if the name is based on one, charter documents of the foreign shareholder, a certified resolution of the foreign shareholder (NOC for similar names, appointment of an authorised representative, subscription details), and main object with NIC code.
steps.time: Name valid 20 days, extendable to 60 days

steps.d: File within the name validity period. Attach MOA and AOA with subscription sheets, address proof of the registered office with owner's NOC and utility bills, ID and address proof of directors and representatives, and INC-9, PAN undertaking and DIR-2. Add address proof of the foreign subscriber, EPF specimen signature, and bank details for the account.
The foreign shareholder signs the subscription sheet physically, and an individual witnesses it.
The Central Registration Centre reviews the file. If in order, it issues the certificate of incorporation.
Check the minimum number of first directors and subscribers. At least one director must be an Indian resident with PAN and DSC. DINs are allotted when the application is approved.
Check the FDI policy for sector caps, prohibited sectors and any need for government approval.

Commonwealth country: notary. Hague Convention country: notary plus apostille. Other countries: notary plus authentication by the Indian embassy or consulate. A person who visited India on a business visa to incorporate is exempt. Identity and address proofs, foreign company's incorporation certificate, MOA and AOA signed abroad all need this.

forms.deadline: Before Part B; name valid 20 days

forms.purpose: Declaration of subscribers and first directors that they have no fraud or conviction history
GST, ESIC, EPF, professional tax, bank account and shops registration

checklist: MOA and AOA with signed subscription sheets
ID and address proof of directors
Indian resident director with PAN and DSC

meetings.title: Board meeting of the foreign shareholder

resolutions.title: Foreign shareholder: subscribing to the new company
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT [name of foreign body corporate] subscribe to [number] equity shares of face value Rs. [amount] each in {co}, a company to be incorporated in India, for Rs. [amount in Rs.]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name], [designation], be appointed as authorised representative and be authorised to sign the subscription sheets and all incorporation documents. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the company gives its no-objection to use of the name '[name]' where it is similar to its own name.

flags: The reference note does not name SPICe+ attachments e-MOA (INC-33) and e-AOA (INC-34); check whether they are used.
The reference note's note on first directors getting DIN on approval applies to those who do not already hold one.
The 20-day name validity extendable to 60 days is as in the reference note; verify the current rule.
Foreign investment reporting under FEMA is not covered.

items: Check the Act for the minimum number of first directors and subscribers. The application must name at least one Indian resident director, who has a valid PAN and digital signature.
The first directors get their DINs when the application is approved.
Check the FDI policy for sector limits, prohibited sectors and any need for prior government approval.

Attesting foreign documents: from a Commonwealth country, a notary public of that country attests them; from a Hague Apostille country, a notary attests and the document is apostilled; from any other country, a notary attests and the Indian Embassy or Consulate authenticates. If the subscriber or director visited India on a valid business visa to set up the company, these steps are not needed.

Notarise, apostille or consularise as applicable: proof of identity and address of the foreign national, the foreign body corporate's certificate of incorporation, the Memorandum and Articles, and any document signed outside India. The place of signing decides which applies.
File the application on the MCA portal at www.mca.gov.in.

title: Buy-back of shares up to 10% by board approval
law: Sections 68, 96, 100 and 173; Rule 17 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014; SEBI (Buy-back of Securities) Regulations, 2018; SEBI Listing Regulations 29, 30 and 46(3); SS-1
summary: A buy-back of 10% or less of paid-up equity capital and free reserves is approved by the board alone, followed by public announcement, escrow, offer, payment and cancellation.
when: When a listed or other company wants a small buy-back without a shareholder resolution.
applies: Mainly listed companies; private companies use only the Companies Act steps

steps.d: The Articles must allow buy-back. If not, change them to match the Act.
A listed company gives the exchange prior intimation of the board meeting, at least 2 working days ahead, not counting the notice day and meeting day.
Pass the buy-back resolution. At the meeting approve financial statements not older than 6 months, the letter of offer, and authority to sign SH-9, SH-8 and SH-11.
A listed company sends the outcome to the exchange within 30 minutes of the meeting end and posts it on its website within 2 working days.
File the board resolution with the Registrar with fees.
A listed company files a copy of the resolution with SEBI and the exchanges.
steps.time: Within 2 working days of the resolution

steps.d: Publish in one English national daily, one Hindi national daily and one regional daily with wide circulation where the registered office is. Include Schedule II disclosures and the record date. File a copy with SEBI and the exchanges with fees, and place it on the websites of the exchanges, merchant banker and company.
steps.time: Within 2 working days of the resolution

steps.d: Before the buy-back, file Form SH-9 signed by at least two directors, one being the managing director.

Before the buy-back file with the Registrar a dated letter of offer in Form SH-8, signed by at least two directors including the MD, with promoter details, auditor's declaration, certified board resolution and 3 years audited accounts. Add other attachments as they apply. Within 2 working days of the record date, file the Schedule III letter of offer and the merchant banker's certificate with SEBI.
steps.time: Before the buy-back; 2 working days from record date

steps.d: Appoint a merchant banker for the buy-back.

Deposit within 2 working days of the public announcement, before the offer opens. If consideration is up to Rs. 100 crore, deposit 25%. Above that, 25% of the first 100 crore and 10% of the rest. It may be cash or bank deposits, a bank guarantee, liquid equity shares or securities, government securities, gilt or overnight mutual fund units, or a mix.

Open the offer no later than 4 working days after the record date. Keep it open for at least 15 and at most 30 days. Send the letter of offer with the tender form. Accept on entitlement as of the record date, split into a reserved small-holder category and a general category, with extra tenders accepted pro rata in each.

Promptly after closing, open a special account and deposit enough, together with up to 90% of the escrow balance, to cover the full consideration. Verify offers, pay those accepted and return the rest.

Destroy certificates before a merchant banker and secretarial auditor by the 15th of the next month, and extinguish all securities within 7 days after the buy-back period. Within 7 days of that, send a compliance certificate verified by the registrar (or merchant banker), two directors including the MD and the statutory auditor. Give details to the exchanges within the same 7 days. Keep the register of buy-backs. File SH-11 with the Registrar (and SEBI if listed). Within 2 days of the period's expiry publish a national newspaper notice showing number, price and total amount, holders of above 1%, and the change in capital and shareholding.

checklist: Buy-back within 10% of paid-up equity and free reserves
Audited financials not older than 6 months
Board resolution with SH-8, SH-9 and SH-11 authority
Letter of offer and tender forms sent

meetings.title: Board meeting to approve the buy-back
meetings.notice_days: At least 7 days (SS-1); 2 working days' exchange intimation if listed

resolutions.title: Approval of buy-back of up to 10%
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT pursuant to Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, Rule 17 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 and, where applicable, the SEBI (Buy-back of Securities) Regulations, 2018, {co} buy back up to [number] fully paid equity shares of Rs. [face value] each at Rs. [price] per share for a total of Rs. [amount in Rs.], not exceeding 10% of the paid-up equity capital and free reserves as per the audited accounts for [period]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the record date be [date] and [name of merchant banker] be appointed merchant banker.

resolutions.title: Authority for solvency declaration, offer letter and filings
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT the Directors approve the financial statements for the period ended [date], the letter of offer and the public announcement. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name], Managing Director, and [name], Director, be authorised to sign the declaration of solvency in Form SH-9, the letter of offer in Form SH-8 and the return in Form SH-11. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name], Company Secretary, be authorised to make all filings with the Registrar, SEBI and the stock exchanges.

docs.title: Public announcement of buy-back
paras: {co}: Public announcement for the buy-back of up to [number] equity shares at Rs. [price] per share, approved by the Board on [date].
Disclosures under Schedule II: [purpose, size and price of buy-back, record date, process, promoter intentions, details of merchant banker and registrar]. The record date is [date].
Issued by [name of merchant banker] on behalf of {co}. Dated [date].

docs.title: Post buy-back public advertisement
paras: {co} has completed its buy-back. Number of securities bought: [number]. Price: Rs. [price] each. Total amount: Rs. [amount in Rs.].
Holders from whom more than 1% of securities were acquired: [details]. Capital structure and shareholding before and after the buy-back: [table].

flags: The reference note cites 'Regulation 17' of the Companies Rules; it should be Rule 17. Sections 96 and 100 relate to AGM and EGM, which a board-only buy-back does not need; check relevance.

The sequence looks off: the merchant banker must be appointed before the public announcement and record date, not after step 9. The letter of offer timing (2 working days from the record date) is also unclear; under the SEBI Regulations the draft letter of offer goes to SEBI shortly after the public announcement. Verify against Regulations 7 and 9.
Offer period of 15 to 30 days and payment within 5 working days look like old or mixed rules. The SEBI 2018 tender offer period is shorter (about 10 working days) and payment time may differ. Verify.
SEBI Regulations apply only to listed companies. The reference note's 'not applicable to private companies' section lists the listed-only steps (exchange intimation, outcome, public announcement).
The reference note says destruction by the 15th of the next month and extinguishment in 7 days; confirm against Regulation 11 and Section 68(7).
private: A listed company has extra duties that a private company does not: intimating the exchange at least 2 working days before the Board meeting, sending the Board outcome within 30 minutes of the meeting end and putting it on the website within 2 working days (Regulations 30 and 46(3)), and making the public announcement in one English national daily, one Hindi national daily and one regional language daily within 2 working days of the Board resolution, with a copy to SEBI and the exchanges.

title: Transferring demat shares of a private company
law: Section 56 of the Companies Act, 2013; Articles of Association; NSDL circular on private company transfers
summary: A shareholder of a private company transfers demat shares off-market after the company gives written consent, using a delivery instruction slip with the depository participant.
when: When a shareholder sells or gifts demat shares of a private limited company.
applies: Private companies with shares in demat form

steps.d: Check the Articles for any restriction or condition on transfer, and follow it.

The seller gives written notice of the intended transfer. The board follows the Articles and approves or refuses. If it approves, the company issues a written no-objection in the format of the NSDL circular dated 3 June 2025. NSDL requires it to go to the DP before processing. CDSL has no such rule yet, but follow the same practice.
The parties agree the transfer. The shares must already be in demat form and both must hold active demat accounts with a DP of NSDL or CDSL, whichever the company has joined.
Value the shares as the Articles say. If silent, the board may fix or approve the value when it gives consent. The buyer pays by NEFT, RTGS or cheque.
The seller gives the DP a completed delivery instruction slip with the company's no-objection and any other papers needed.
The DP checks the DIS and sends it to the company or its registrar for validation. After confirmation the DP debits the seller's account and credits the buyer's account.
The buyer informs the company once the credit shows. The company updates its Register of Members straight away, and the board notes the transfer at its next meeting.
steps.time: Register updated immediately; board at next meeting

meetings.title: Board meeting to consent to transfer
meetings.notice_days: As per SS-1 (7 days) or by circular

resolutions.title: Consent to transfer of demat shares
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, in accordance with the Articles of Association of {co} and Section 56 of the Companies Act, 2013, consent be given to [name of transferor] to transfer [number] equity shares held in demat account no. [DP ID and client ID] to [name of transferee] at Rs. [price] per share. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name], Director / Company Secretary, be authorised to issue the no-objection letter to the transferor and its depository participant and to update the Register of Members.

docs.title: No-objection letter for transfer of shares
paras: To the Depository Participant, [name]. {co} has no objection to the transfer of [number] equity shares (ISIN [ISIN]) from [name of transferor], demat account [number], to [name of transferee], demat account [number].
The board approved this transfer on [date] in line with the Articles of Association. Signed: [name], Director / Company Secretary, [date].

flags: The reference note cites NSDL circular NSDL/POLICY/2025/0071 dated 3 June 2025; verify the number and date and whether CDSL has since adopted a similar rule.
Stamp duty on demat transfers is not mentioned; it is collected through the DP. Verify the current rate.
Section 56 is cited alone; a private company's restriction on transfer arises from its Articles (Section 2(68)).
private: As the shares are already in demat form, the company need not issue or endorse share certificates for the transfer. A private unlisted company executes the transfer off-market, with no stock exchange involved.

title: Transmission of shares after the nominee dies
law: Sections 56 and 72; SEBI Listing Regulations on transmission (documents for transmission)
summary: Where both the shareholder and the nominee have died, legal heirs claim the shares by sending death proofs and other documents to the registrar, with extra papers depending on share value.
when: When a shareholder and the nominee have both died and heirs want the shares in their names.
applies: Listed and public companies through the registrar; private companies follow their Articles

steps.d: The claimants write to the company or registrar about the deaths of the shareholder and the nominee, stating how each claimant is related to the shareholder.

Enclose death certificates of both, the transmission request form, share certificates (physical) or demat account details, the claimants' demat details, self-certified ID and address proof (PAN, Aadhaar, passport) and bank details.
The registrar checks the documents.

Where shares are worth more than Rs. 5 lakh in physical form or Rs. 15 lakh in demat form, the claimants also give an attested or notarised copy of a letter of administration, probate or succession certificate from a competent court.
steps.time: Value above Rs. 5 lakh (physical) or Rs. 15 lakh (demat)

steps.d: Where shares are worth up to Rs. 5 lakh (physical) or Rs. 15 lakh (demat) and no court document exists, the claimants give a notarised indemnity bond on stamp paper and a no-objection from every legal heir who is not claiming.
steps.time: Value up to Rs. 5 lakh (physical) or Rs. 15 lakh (demat)

steps.d: After receipt of all papers, shares are credited to the claimants' demat account.
The company updates its records to show the claimants as holders.

checklist: Death certificates of shareholder and nominee
Indemnity bond on stamp paper (below threshold)

docs.title: Indemnity bond for transmission of shares
paras: I/We, [names of claimants], residing at [addresses], are legal heirs of the late [name of shareholder] and the late [name of nominee], holders/nominee of [number] shares of {co}, folio / DP ID [number].
I/We request that these shares be transmitted in my/our name(s). I/We indemnify {co} and its registrar against all claims, losses and costs arising from the transmission to me/us.
Signed: [names], [date]. Notarised on stamp paper of Rs. [value].

docs.title: No-objection from legal heir
paras: I, [name], a legal heir of the late [name of shareholder], have no objection to the transmission of [number] shares of {co} (folio / DP ID [number]) in favour of [names of claimants]. Signed: [name], [date].

flags: The reference note says the Act has no specific process for death of a nominee. When the nominee dies, the nomination lapses and the heirs claim by transmission; the Articles and SEBI rules govern the process.
The Rs. 5 lakh and Rs. 15 lakh thresholds come from SEBI rules that have changed over time; verify current limits.
For private companies, the Articles decide the process; the court-certificate requirement does not bind them.
private: The need to produce letters of administration, probate or a succession certificate comes from the SEBI listing rules, so it does not apply to a private company. Its Articles can set how shares are transmitted without asking for these documents.

title: Removing an auditor and filling a casual vacancy
law: Sections 139(1), 139(8), 139(11), 140(1), 140(5), 141 and 447; Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014
summary: Covers how a company removes its auditor before the term ends (with Central Government approval and a special resolution, or by NCLT order for fraud) and how a casual vacancy in the auditor's office is filled.
when: When the company wants to end an auditor's five-year term early, or when the auditor resigns, dies or becomes disqualified.
applies: All companies; government companies follow the CAG route for vacancies

steps.d: Hold a board meeting to consider removing the auditor before the term ends. Give the auditor a fair chance to be heard before the board decides. Authorise a director or the Company Secretary to apply for approval.
File an application stating the reasons for removal, and give the auditor a copy. The Regional Director acts for the Central Government.
steps.time: Within 30 days of the board resolution

steps.d: The Regional Director hears the company and the auditor. If satisfied with the reasons, the Regional Director approves the removal.

steps.t: Special resolution at a general meeting
steps.d: On getting the approval, call an AGM or EGM and pass a special resolution removing the auditor. Circulate the auditor's written representation if it arrives in time; otherwise the auditor may ask for it to be read at the meeting.
steps.time: Meeting within 60 days of the approval

steps.d: File the special resolution with the Registrar, attaching a certified copy of it and the Regional Director's order.
steps.time: Within the time prescribed for MGT-14

steps.d: Where the auditor has acted fraudulently or helped others do so, the NCLT can direct a change of auditor. It may act on its own, or on an application from the Central Government or a person concerned. The auditor gets a hearing and the NCLT inquires. If the Central Government applies, the NCLT must decide within 15 days.
docs: Application to NCLT with details of fraud

steps.d: The auditor against whom a final order is made cannot be appointed auditor of any company for five years from the order. The auditor may also face action under Section 447.
A casual vacancy arises on resignation, death or disqualification. Check the cause because the filling route differs. Government companies follow the CAG route.

Place the proposed appointment before the Audit Committee (if the company needs one) and then the Board. Check the person is eligible under Section 141. Where the cause is not resignation, the Board appoints.
docs: Consent and eligibility certificate of auditor

steps.d: If the vacancy came from resignation, call an EGM to approve the Board's appointment.
steps.time: Within 3 months of the Board's recommendation

steps.d: The CAG fills the vacancy within 30 days. If the CAG does not, the Board fills it within the next 30 days.
The resigning auditor files a statement of reasons with the company and the Registrar (and the CAG for government companies). Quote its SRN when filing ADT-1 for the new auditor.

steps.t: Inform the Registrar of the appointment
steps.d: File notice of the new auditor's appointment.
steps.time: Within 15 days of the Board or general meeting making the appointment

steps.d: The auditor appointed in a casual vacancy holds office until the next AGM. At that AGM the members appoint an auditor for a full term (usually five years, subject to rotation).

forms.purpose: Application to the Central Government (Regional Director) for approval to remove an auditor
forms.deadline: Within 30 days of the board resolution

forms.purpose: Filing of the special resolution removing the auditor

forms.deadline: Within 15 days of the meeting making the appointment

checklist: Auditor given a chance to be heard
ADT-2 with reasons and copy to auditor
Notice of meeting and special resolution within 60 days of order
Auditor's representation circulated or read out
Auditor consent and Section 141 eligibility certificate

meetings.title: Board meeting to seek removal of auditor
meetings.notice_days: As per Section 173 and SS-1 (at least 7 days; shorter if all directors agree)

meetings.title: General meeting to remove auditor
meetings.notice_days: At least 21 clear days (shorter with consent of members as the Act allows)

meetings.title: Board meeting to fill casual vacancy
General meeting to approve casual-vacancy appointment

resolutions.title: Proposal to remove the auditor and apply to the Regional Director
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT the Board, having heard [name of auditor] on [date], considers it necessary to remove [name of auditor], statutory auditor of {co}, before the end of the term, for the reasons placed before the meeting. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT, as required by Section 140(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, an application in Form ADT-2 be made to the Regional Director for approval, within 30 days of this resolution. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director / Company Secretary] is authorised to sign and file the application and do all things needed.

resolutions.title: Removal of the statutory auditor
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 140(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 and the approval of the Regional Director dated [date], [name of auditor], Chartered Accountants (Firm Reg. No. [number]), be and is hereby removed from the office of statutory auditor of {co} with effect from [date]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Board is authorised to appoint a new auditor under the Act and to file Form MGT-14 and all other forms.
resolutions.explanatory: This is a special resolution under Section 140(1). The Regional Director approved the removal on [date]. The auditor was heard by the Board and has the right to make a written representation to members. No director is interested in this resolution except as a member.

resolutions.title: Appointment of auditor to fill a casual vacancy
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 139(8) of the Companies Act, 2013 and on the recommendation of the Audit Committee, [name of auditor], Chartered Accountants (Firm Reg. No. [number]), who have given their consent and a certificate of eligibility under Section 141, be and are hereby appointed statutory auditor of {co} to fill the casual vacancy caused by [resignation / death / disqualification] of [name of previous auditor], to hold office until the conclusion of the next annual general meeting, at a remuneration of Rs. [amount]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director / Company Secretary] is authorised to file Form ADT-1 within 15 days and do all things needed. [Where the vacancy arose from resignation: RESOLVED FURTHER THAT an extraordinary general meeting be called within three months to approve this appointment.]

resolutions.title: Approval of auditor appointed in casual vacancy
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 139(8)(i) of the Companies Act, 2013, the appointment of [name of auditor], Chartered Accountants (Firm Reg. No. [number]), made by the Board on [date] to fill the casual vacancy caused by the resignation of [name of previous auditor], be and is hereby approved, to hold office until the conclusion of the next annual general meeting at a remuneration of Rs. [amount].
resolutions.explanatory: The vacancy arose from the resignation of the previous auditor. Section 139(8) requires members to approve the Board's appointment at a general meeting held within three months of the Board's recommendation. The proposed auditor has given consent and eligibility certificate under Section 141.

docs.title: Notice to auditor of hearing before removal
paras: To: [name of auditor], [address]

{co} proposes to remove you from the office of statutory auditor before the end of your term under Section 140(1) of the Companies Act, 2013. The Board will consider this on [date] at [time] at [place]. The reasons are: [reasons].
You may attend and be heard, or send written submissions by [date]. For {co}: [name], [designation].

flags: The reference note treats removal and casual vacancy together. After a removal the company still has to appoint a new auditor (Section 140(4) and ADT-1); the reference note does not spell this out.
The reference note says MGT-14 is filed 'within the prescribed time'. The usual period is 30 days from the resolution; verify.

The reference note says ADT-1 is due within 15 days of the Board meeting or the general meeting. For resignation cases the safer course is to count from the general meeting that approves the appointment; verify against Rule 4.
Section 139(8) as quoted gives the Board 30 days to fill a vacancy. The reference note is silent on what happens if the 30 days lapse; consider condonation or an early meeting.
Private and small companies may have different treatment under notifications; check current exemptions.

title: Appointing a person other than a retiring director at a general meeting
law: Sections 152, 160, 164 and 170; Rule 13 of the Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014; Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014; SS-1 and SS-2
summary: A new person, who is not a retiring director, can be appointed by members at a general meeting if a written notice of candidature and the deposit reach the company 14 days before the meeting.
when: When a member or the candidate wants to propose someone other than a retiring director for election as director.
applies: Public companies; the notice and deposit steps do not apply to private companies

steps.d: Confirm the person is not a retiring director under Section 152 and is not disqualified under Section 164. Such a person can be appointed at any general meeting if the conditions are met.
The candidate, or a member proposing the candidate, signs a written notice and delivers it to the registered office.
steps.time: At least 14 days before the general meeting

steps.d: The notice must come with a deposit of Rs. 1,00,000 or a higher amount if prescribed.
No deposit is needed if the person is an independent director, is recommended by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee, or is recommended by the Board where no such committee is required.
Tell members about the candidature as the rules require. The reference note also mentions placing the notice on the company's website, if it has one.

Add a resolution for the appointment to the notice. The explanatory statement and notes must state that the candidature notice and deposit were received under Section 160. Give a short profile of the person as the Secretarial Standards ask.
Members vote on the resolution. Record votes for and against clearly in the minutes.
If the resolution passes, file the appointment with the Registrar. If it fails, no filing is needed.
Refund the deposit if the person is elected, or gets 25% or more of the valid votes cast (on a show of hands or a poll).
Enter the director's details in the Register of Directors and Key Managerial Personnel.

checklist: Notice of candidature signed and received 14 days before the meeting
Deposit of Rs. 1,00,000 received (or exemption confirmed)
Explanatory statement states receipt of notice and deposit
Minutes record votes for and against

meetings.title: Annual or extraordinary general meeting to appoint a director

resolutions.title: Appointment of a director
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Sections 152 and 160 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the rules made under it, [name of person] (DIN [number]), in respect of whom the company has received notice in writing from [a member / the candidate] under Section 160, be and is hereby appointed a director of {co}, [liable to retire by rotation]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director / Company Secretary] is authorised to file Form DIR-12 and do all things needed.
resolutions.explanatory: The company received notice dated [date] from [name of member / candidate] proposing [name] as a director, along with a deposit of Rs. [amount] [or: no deposit is needed as the person is an independent director / recommended by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee / recommended by the Board]. A short profile of [name] is: [profile]. Notice under Section 160 has been given to members. None of the directors, except as members, is interested in this resolution.

docs.title: Notice of candidature for director
paras: To: The Board of Directors, {co}, [registered office address]

I, [name of member / candidate], give notice under Section 160 of the Companies Act, 2013 of [my candidature / my intention to propose [name of person]] for the office of director at the general meeting to be held on [date]. A deposit of Rs. 1,00,000 is enclosed.
Signed: [name], [date].

flags: Under Section 160(2) and Rule 13 the company must inform members of the candidature at least 7 days before the meeting by individual notice or by newspaper advertisement, and also place it on its website, if any. The reference note mentions only the website; verify and do all of them.
The reference note does not list the director's DIN and consent in Form DIR-2 (Sections 152(5) and 153). Obtain them before the meeting.
Deposit amount of Rs. 1,00,000 is stated as 'or such higher amount as prescribed'; the Act sets Rs. 1,00,000, so verify any change.
The reference note says private companies skip this procedure; they appoint under their Articles without Section 160 notice.
private: This section does not apply to a private company.

title: Borrowing beyond paid-up capital and free reserves (public company)
law: Sections 179(1), 180(1)(c), 180(2), 188, 102, 117 and 77; Rule 15 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014; Rule 3 of the Companies (Registration of Charges) Rules, 2014; SS-1 and SS-2
summary: A public company needs a special resolution of members before the Board borrows more than the total of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium.
when: When existing and proposed borrowings together exceed paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium.
applies: Public companies; private companies are exempt from the special resolution (GSR 464(E) dated 5 June 2015)

steps.d: See whether the Articles, the Memorandum or any general meeting resolution allow the company to borrow.
If there is no restriction, add the proposed borrowing to existing borrowings and compare with paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium.

steps.t: Decide if a special resolution is needed
steps.d: If the total is higher, a special resolution under Section 180(1)(c) is needed. Leave out temporary loans: repayable on demand or within six months, from bankers in the ordinary course, such as cash credit and bill discounting. Loans for capital expenditure do not count as temporary.
Issue notice for a board meeting to approve the borrowing and to call a general meeting for the special resolution.
Approve the borrowing, subject to members' approval, and approve the general meeting notice.
Send the notice with the explanatory statement under Section 102, as the Board approved.
Hold the meeting and pass the special resolution. It must state the total amount up to which the Board may borrow.
File the special resolution with the Registrar.
If the borrowing is secured, file the charge with the Registrar.
steps.time: Within 30 days of creating the charge

steps.d: Where the lender is a related party, pass a board resolution if the borrowing is under 10% of turnover. The board agenda must give the party's name and relationship, the nature, duration and terms of the contract, its value, any advance, and the other items in Rule 15(1). An interested director must stay out during the discussion.

steps.t: Related party borrowing at or above 10% of turnover
steps.d: Get prior approval of members by ordinary resolution. The notice needs an explanatory statement with the Rule 15(3) particulars. Interested members cannot vote on it.

forms.purpose: Filing of special resolution under Section 180(1)(c)
Registration of charge for secured borrowing
forms.deadline: Within 30 days of creation of the charge

checklist: Articles and Memorandum checked for borrowing power
Temporary loans excluded from the calculation
General meeting notice with Section 102 statement
Special resolution states the total borrowing limit
CHG-1 filed within 30 days for secured loans
Related party disclosures and conflict recusal (if applicable)

meetings.title: Board meeting to approve borrowing and call general meeting

resolutions.title: Board approval of proposed borrowing
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 179(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, and subject to the approval of the members under Section 180(1)(c), the Board approves borrowing of Rs. [amount] from [name of lender] on the terms placed before the meeting. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director / Company Secretary] is authorised to negotiate and sign the documents, create security, and file Forms MGT-14 and CHG-1.

resolutions.title: Call of general meeting and approval of notice
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT a general meeting of {co} be held on [date] at [time] at [place / video conference] to consider a special resolution under Section 180(1)(c), and that the notice and explanatory statement under Section 102 placed before the meeting are approved and may be sent to the members.

resolutions.title: Authority to borrow above paid-up capital and free reserves
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 180(1)(c) and other applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, consent of the members be and is hereby given to the Board to borrow, from time to time, such sums as it thinks fit, even if the total borrowing then exceeds the aggregate of the paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium of {co}, provided the total amount borrowed and outstanding shall not exceed Rs. [amount in figures and words]. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Board is authorised to take all steps needed, including creating security under Section 180(1)(a).
resolutions.explanatory: Section 180(1)(c) needs members' consent by special resolution before the Board borrows beyond the aggregate of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium. The present paid-up capital is Rs. [amount], free reserves Rs. [amount] and securities premium Rs. [amount]; existing borrowings are Rs. [amount]. The resolution states the ceiling of Rs. [amount]. No director or key managerial person is interested, except as a member.

resolutions.title: Approval of borrowing from a related party
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 15 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, approval of the members be and is hereby given to borrow Rs. [amount] from [name of related party], a related party under Section 2(76), on the terms placed before the meeting. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT [name of director / Company Secretary] is authorised to do all things needed.
resolutions.explanatory: The related party is [name], whose relationship with the company is [nature]. The loan is for [duration] at interest of [rate] with other material terms: [terms]. The value is Rs. [amount], which is [percentage]% of turnover. Interested directors and members must not vote.

flags: The related-party steps are needed only if the lender is a related party. Section 188(1) lists specific transactions; borrowing is not one of them, and the Rule 15(3) thresholds are on those listed items. The reference note's '10% of turnover' test for borrowing looks doubtful. Check whether Section 188 applies at all, and check Sections 185 and 186 and the deposit rules (Section 73) for loans from directors or members.
The reference note does not mention that the Board's power to borrow arises under Section 179(3)(d) and that board resolutions on borrowing are filed in MGT-14 (Section 117(3)(g)). Verify.
The reference note refers to Section 188(1)(d) and its provisos; Section 188(1)(d) deals with leasing of property, so the citation may be misplaced.
Private companies: the special resolution is not needed, but check the Articles.
private: A private company need not pass a special resolution here (exemption notification GSR 464(E) of 5 June 2015).

title: Setting up the Audit, Nomination and Remuneration, and Stakeholders Relationship Committees
law: Sections 177 and 178; Rule 6 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014; Rule 4 of the Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014; Section 149; Secretarial Standard 1
summary: Sets out which companies must form the three board committees, who sits on each, what the Board must decide, and what must be disclosed.
when: When a public company meets the size or listing test, or has more than 1,000 security holders, and must constitute these committees.
applies: Listed companies and public companies meeting the size tests; not private companies

steps.t: Check who must form the committees
steps.d: Audit Committee and Nomination and Remuneration Committee: every listed company, and public companies with paid-up capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, or turnover of Rs. 100 crore or more, or outstanding loans, debentures and deposits above Rs. 50 crore in total. Stakeholders Relationship Committee: a board of a company with more than 1,000 security holders at any time in the year.
Hold a board meeting to appoint at least two independent directors qualified under Section 149, following the other provisions of the Act.
Pass a resolution forming a committee of at least three directors, with independent directors in the majority. Name the chairperson.
Fix how often it meets, how meetings are called, the quorum and other terms.

Fix the terms of reference. At least: recommending auditors and their pay, reviewing auditor independence and performance, examining financial statements and the auditor's report, approving related party transactions, scrutinising inter-corporate loans and investments, valuing undertakings or assets, evaluating internal financial controls and risk management, and monitoring the end use of funds from public offers. More duties may be added.

Follow Secretarial Standard 1 for its meetings. Disclose its composition in the Board's report, and any Board decision not to accept its recommendation with reasons. The chairperson, or another member authorised by the chair, attends general meetings.

Pass a resolution forming a committee of three or more non-executive directors, at least half independent, and name the chairperson. Three independent directors can form the committee alone. With only two independent directors, appoint one more non-executive director. The company's chairperson may be a member but cannot chair it.

Fix meeting rules and terms of reference: identify people fit to be directors or senior management and recommend their appointment and removal; decide how Board, committee and director performance is evaluated; set criteria for qualifications, positive attributes and independence, and recommend a pay policy for directors, KMP and employees in line with Section 178(4).

Put the policy on the company's website, if any. In the Board's report under Section 134 give its main features, any changes and the web address. Follow SS-1. The chairperson or an authorised member attends general meetings.

Pass a resolution forming a committee with a non-executive director as chairperson and other members as the Board decides. No minimum size is fixed; at least three directors with one independent is good practice.
Fix meeting rules. Its main job is to consider and resolve grievances of security holders. Follow SS-1; the chairperson or authorised member attends general meetings.

checklist: Applicability test done for each committee
At least two independent directors appointed (Audit Committee)
Audit Committee has at least three directors, independents in majority
NRC has three or more non-executive directors, at least half independent
SRC chair is a non-executive director
Quorum, frequency and mode of meetings fixed

meetings.title: Board meeting to constitute the committees
meetings.notice_days: As per Section 173 and SS-1 (at least 7 days; shorter if all directors agree)

resolutions.title: Constitution of the Audit Committee
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 177 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 6 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, an Audit Committee of {co} be constituted with [name], [name] and [name] as members, a majority being independent directors, and [name] as chairperson. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the committee shall meet at least [number] times a year, with a quorum of [number] members, and its terms of reference shall be as placed before the meeting and shall include the matters in Section 177(4).

resolutions.title: Constitution of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 178(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a Nomination and Remuneration Committee of {co} be constituted with [name], [name] and [name], all non-executive directors, at least half being independent, and [name] as chairperson. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT its terms of reference shall include the matters in Section 178(2), (3) and (4), and that the remuneration policy approved by it be placed on the website of the company and disclosed in the Board's report.

resolutions.title: Constitution of the Stakeholders Relationship Committee
resolutions.text: RESOLVED THAT, pursuant to Section 178(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, a Stakeholders Relationship Committee of {co} be constituted with [name], a non-executive director, as chairperson and [names] as members. RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the committee shall consider and resolve grievances of security holders and shall meet at least [number] times a year, with a quorum of [number] members.

flags: The reference note cites Section 178(1) for the Stakeholders Relationship Committee; the duty is in Section 178(5). The 1,000-holder test applies to all companies with such holders, not only public companies, so check whether the exemption for private companies stated in the reference note matches the Act.

The reference note says appoint at least two independent directors. Rule 4 sets this at two for unlisted public companies; listed companies need one-third of the board and SEBI (LODR) rules (such as three independent directors in the Audit Committee) apply. Verify.
Rule 6 and notifications give some exemptions (for example wholly owned subsidiaries, dormant companies, joint ventures). Not mentioned in the reference note.

Audit Committee requirement in Section 177(2) is that independent directors form the majority; the reference note's phrasing is consistent, but SEBI rules for listed companies are stricter (two-thirds independent). Verify.
Appointment of independent directors itself needs board and shareholder approval; see the separate procedure.
private: A private company need not have an Audit Committee, a Nomination and Remuneration Committee or a Stakeholders Relationship Committee.
